title: More Treatments More Problems: Designing the 2026 American Causal Inference Conference Data Challenge
summary: This paper documents the design of the 2026 American Causal Inference Conference (ACIC) Data Challenge, which uses a large set of simulations to evaluate the performance of a wide variety of causal inference estimators chosen and implemented by challenge participants. Unlike previous ACIC Data Challenges, which tended to mimic observational studies with a single binary treatment, the 2026 Data Challenge focused on randomized control trials with five arms (one control and four active treatments) to isolate key estimation challenges that arise when simultaneously estimating multiple treatment effects. We created 9,000 distinct synthetic populations corresponding to 18 distinct settings to explore variation in performance corresponding to patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity and response surface specifications. From each population, a sample of n = 1,000 was drawn for participants to estimate individual, subgroup, sample, and population-level treatment effects and identify the optimal treatment arm at each level. We describe several strategies used to generate the data to prevent Challenge participants from exploiting structural sim across datasets and ``gaming the system.'' By detailing these simulation design considerations and data generation choices, this paper provides a framework for conducting large-scale, unconfounded synthetic benchmark studies to rigorously evaluate multi-treatment causal inference procedures.

title: PICKLES: Covariance-Preconditioned Kinetic Langevin Ensemble Sampler
summary: We propose a covariance-preconditioned kinetic Langevin ensemble sampler named PICKLES. This is a kinetic analogue of the affine invariant interacting Langevin dynamics (ALDI). PICKLES uses a rectangular covariance square root as a preconditioner to avoid computing matrix inverses or square roots, leading to position and momentum variables of different dimensions. Theoretically, the continuous-time dynamics are ergodic under mild regularity and growth conditions on the potential, assuming $N>d+1$ particles and a full-rank initial ensemble. We discretize PICKLES using BAOAB or OBABO splitting, with the latter convenient for Metropolization. For Gaussian targets at stationarity, we demonstrate that Metropolized PICKLES achieves an integration step size scaling of $d^{-1/4}$ to achieve fixed acceptance probabilities, as the ensemble size and dimension increase at a fixed ratio. This matches the scaling of single particle Metropolized Hamiltonian and kinetic samplers. Numerical experiments compare sampling efficiency and estimation error with non-preconditioned, overdamped, and single-chain counterparts, demonstrating improved efficiency per gradient evaluation. On a Dark Energy Survey Year 1 3x2pt cosmology benchmark, we obtain competitive effective sample size per gradient evaluation compared to a densely preconditioned No-U-Turn Sampler.

title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
summary: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

title: An Unbounded Gap Between Identification and Identifiable Elicitation: Central Moments
summary: For $n\geq2$, two expectation equations identify the mean together with the $n$th central moment. How many coordinates must a report have if a one-observation loss uniquely elicits it and the report determines that moment? We prove that $n$ coordinates are necessary and sufficient among all identifiable intermediaries. The result holds on every open convex set of positive distributions on any $n+1$ distinct real outcomes. It requires no regularity of the loss, report map, identification function, or link. Thus $\operatorname{elic}_{\mathcal I}(μ_n)=n$ while $\operatorname{iden}(μ_n)\leq2$, giving an unbounded gap between identifiable elicitation and indirect identification. This resolves the central-moment conjecture of Frongillo and Kash on the stated domains. The proof constructs a $C^1$ manifold of supporting coefficients from the affine fibers of a convex negative Bayes risk. Translations along that manifold force an $n$-dimensional tangent space. Standardized moments of order at least three have the same exact complexity. The bound also extends to convex distribution classes with a full-dimensional raw-moment image.

title: Computational Taxonomy for visualizing and exploring systems with functional response dynamics: soybean's O2-respiration example
summary: A collective of 1684 O2-respiration curves of 183 dimensions are collected along soybeans' germinating process with 72 covariate feature-measurements. We develop a computational thematic platform for first discovering and exposing heterogeneous typical-shapes and then extracting readable, visible and explainable pattern information with biological implications when comparing between them. Via existing knowledge on seeds of much smaller sizes, such collective of O2-respiration curves are expected to generally embrace the two-stage or sigmoidal patterns. However, due to Soybean's relatively large surface area with harder to control and retain experimental conditions, much diverse and heterogeneous shapes are highly expected. Shannon entropy is applied to capture potential categorical nature across the 183 time-points, while scaled mutual information is used to evaluate pattern-consistency. Three motifs are determined to partition the temporal time-points into three regions: W1 on [1, 20], W2 on [21, 60] and W3 on [61, 183]. Each curve is partitioned into three segments accordingly. Hierarchical cluster algorithm is applied onto these motif-region-specific curve-segments, respectively. Five clusters of shapes on W1 are selected, four on W2 and four on W3. We computationally build a tree-geometry-based Taxonomic Hierarchy to organize these 80 curve-shapes into 15 typical shapes. Then we compare among these typical shapes to extract and display their differences through block-sustained heatmaps. Each focal block is expressed va a network of covariate features to reveal dominant interacting effects of various orders. Scientific explanations and understanding are to be rested on the collected heatmaps and coupled networks collectively.

title: Causal adaptive intensity estimation for non-stationary point processes: a Kalman-kernel duality framework
summary: Estimating the instantaneous conditional intensity of a non-stationary point process from a single realization of discrete event timestamps is a fundamental problem in computational neuroscience, quantitative finance, and network monitoring. Traditional adaptive kernel methods achieve variable bandwidths through Abramson's square-root law, yet existing implementations require non-causal access to the complete event record and incur $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ or at best $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ computational cost. Causal alternatives based on reciprocal inter-arrival times, meanwhile, suffer from systematic divergence under Poisson and bursty arrival dynamics due to Jensen's inequality. This paper addresses both limitations by establishing a formal duality between steady-state Kalman filtering and adaptive exponential kernel smoothing. An endogenous state-space observer is constructed in which Poisson counting statistics dictate the measurement noise ($R \propto λ$) and geometric diffusion governs the process volatility ($Q \propto λ^2$). Under these physically motivated axioms, the algebraic Riccati equation autonomously yields an effective smoothing bandwidth scaling as $τ\propto λ^{-1/2}$, giving a causal, recursive, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per-step realization of square-root adaptive bandwidth scaling. A second-order constant-velocity extension produces a $λ^{-1/4}$ scaling that reduces approximation bias, and a probabilistic dormant-state gating mechanism suppresses phantom intensity leakage during structural zeros. Synthetic benchmarks together with neural and financial data show that the observer adapts across orders of magnitude in intensity with an empirical per-step cost of approximately 30\,$μ$s.

title: Exploiting sparse conditional dependence in remote sensing observing systems
summary: We develop a novel filtering algorithm for remote sensing inverse problems that exploits sparsity in the precision (inverse covariance) matrix arising from conditional independence structures in spatio-temporal satellite data. Motivated by NASA's Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2), Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation (EMIT), and upcoming Explorer for Artemis Geology Lunar and Earth (EAGLE) missions, we formulate a Bayesian inference framework for retrieving atmospheric and surface parameters from hyperspectral radiance measurements. Unlike traditional methods that operate on covariances and ignore spatio-temporal dependencies, our approach models the full spatio-temporal state using sparse Gaussian graphical models, which corresponds to a block-sparse precision matrix. We derive an information filter based on this structure, enabling scalable joint inference over large spatial grids with uncertainty propagation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm in two distinct remote sensing contexts. First, we apply the method to synthetic data configured to mimic the OCO-2 mission, focusing on retrievals of atmospheric CO$_2$, and observe a 50% reduction in CO$_2$ retrieval error compared to single-pixel methods. Then, we evaluate the algorithm using imaging spectroscopy data from the Surface Biology and Geology (SBG) High Frequency Time Series (SHIFT) campaign to retrieve surface reflectance, achieving a 20% reduction in retrieval error relative to baseline approaches.

title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning convex conformity scores that induce flexible, data-adaptive prediction regions. CoCoNet learns the score from held-out data by optimizing prediction-region efficiency while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}}$, based on piecewise-linear scores, and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{ICNN}}$, based on Input Convex Neural Networks. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. The results demonstrate the flexibility of CoCoNet in learning different response types. Across 8 models and 30 multi-dimensional regression tasks, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}\text{-}\ell_1}$ achieve the best efficiencies with average ranks of 1.45 and 2.75, respectively. In particular, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ ranks first on 22 tasks out of 30 in terms of efficiency.

title: Benign Overfitting Property of the Minimum $\ell_q$ -norm Interpolant Estimator in Regression Problem via Feature Space Decomposition
summary: This paper establishes high-probability, non-asymptotic upper bounds for the population excess risk of minimum $\ell_q$-norm interpolating estimators in linear regression, valid for all $1<q<\infty$ under three scenarios: convex concentration, mild moment assumptions and log-concavity. Consequently, we derive sufficient conditions for these estimators to exhibit benign overfitting. Our analysis hinges on a Feature Space Decomposition (FSD) framework, which naturally highlights the self-regularizing properties of minimum norm interpolants as well as the role of alignment between the signal and the features for benign overfitting. From a technical perspective, our approach circumvents the traditionally used Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT) by instead leveraging the Dvoretzky-Milman theorem. We emphasize that the FSD method has the potential to refine standard uniform convergence approaches. Furthermore, the isomorphic Dvoretzky-Milman theorem established herein -- proven under the three scenarios mentioned above -- for the $\ell_q$-norm is of independent mathematical interest.

title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses
summary: A rare 3D human pose in a motion sequence may reflect either a genuine movement or an estimation error, making correction difficult when reference databases contain few comparable examples. We investigate whether local geometric structure can support the recovery and generation of rare configura- tions, using motion-capture sequences from AMASS, which unifies datasets through a common parametric human-body model, together with video-based pose estimates. We develop the cylindrical manifold attention transformer (CMAT), which extends local manifold fitting through geometry- and task- dependent neighborhood weights. For motion correction, Self-Action CMAT draws on comparable windows within a sequence, adjusts their contributions for neighborhood imbalance and temporal dependence, and integrates local geometry with robust temporal regularization. Experiments on perturbed and estimated motions show reductions in position and acceleration errors, with component analyses examining how weighting and temporal processing con- tribute to recovery. The controlled correction comparisons are exploratory and conditional on the selected motion-amplitude bound. For generation, Rarity-preserving CMAT explores locally supported configurations subject to independently calibrated rarity and separation from stored observations. Under common screening criteria, it achieves a higher yield of eligible rare poses than the evaluated generation baselines.

title: Extrinsic MANOVA for Oriented Projective Shapes
summary: For configurations of landmarks reconstructed from camera images, classical projective shape analysis identifies antipodal spherical representatives of projective coordinates, while oriented projective shape (OPS) retains their distinction. In 3D, a fixed oriented-projective coordinate representation of a OPS is point on product of 3D spheres. We develop nonparametric multisample inference for equality of population extrinsic means on this product. Quaternion multiplication helps create a global orthonormal tangent frame field, in which we obtain explicit extrinsic covariance blocks that preserve dependence between registered landmarks. A covariance-weighted MANOVA statistic has a chi-square null limit under nonfocality of distributions and positive-definite extrinsic covariance assumptions. An inverse-free discrepancy has a weighted chi-square limit when covariance matrices may be singular, and centered, groupwise nonparametric bootstrap procedures are justified asymptotically. We apply a fixed-observed-covariance nonparametric bootstrap version of the weighted statistic to 31 seven-landmark facial reconstructions from five subjects. Separate tests at the right inner brow and chin reject equality of the five OPS mean directions after Bonferroni adjustment. The analysis concerns a common mixed-sign frame domain and marginal landmarks; it does not establish pairwise subject differences or a joint six-dimensional facial test.

title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
comment: R and Python package available at https://github.com/danilosarti/lepidoptera
summary: lepidoptera is an open-source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. A pre-built mechanism library covers all nine combinations of continuous, categorical, and ordinal parent and child types, removing the need for users to implement type-specific sampling from scratch. A vine copula mechanism estimates the full joint dependence structure from observed data using pair-copula constructions and the Rosenblatt conditional-simulation algorithm, supporting over twenty copula families. Individual-level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population-level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre-fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. Three worked illustrations spanning clinical trial planning, emergency-ward capacity analysis, and epidemiological mediation analysis demonstrate the package's scope.

title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
summary:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO).
  Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors.
  Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead.
  Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

title: Asymptotic Normality of the Hill Estimator in Linear Preferential Attachment
summary: We prove asymptotic normality of the Hill estimator based on the largest $k_n$ degrees in a homogeneous linear preferential attachment graph with $n$ vertices. Each new vertex sends a fixed number $m\ge1$ of edges sequentially to older vertices, with attachment weight $d+δ$ and fixed $δ>-m$. Let $α=m/(2m+δ)$. For every deterministic sequence $k_n\to\infty$ satisfying $\sqrt{k_n}(k_n/n)^α\to0$, the estimator, centered at $α$ and multiplied by $\sqrt{k_n}$, converges to a centered normal law with an explicit variance strictly smaller than $α^2$. The reduction relative to the Hill variance for independent observations separates into contributions from the different degree laws at different birth times and from competition for new edges. The contribution from competition is $1/m$ times that from different birth times. Representations using Gamma and beta functions give a consistent standard error and a studentized normal limit. The proof uses martingales indexed by edge attachments and comparisons with independent pure-birth processes, while retaining the integer degrees and their ties.

title: Logistic vegetation trajectories and their implications for land surface phenology
summary: Vegetation trajectories describe canopy development and underpin phenological metrics, including the start and end of the growing season. We derive a generalized logistic function (GLF) to represent canopy growth under explicit assumptions: exponential development combined with a Michaelis-Menten-type saturating response yields an ordinary logistic function, and a power transformation introduces asymmetry. Using the GLF as a common mathematical basis, we relate trajectory shape to phenological metrics and date uncertainty. We derive shape-dependent relative thresholds for derivative-defined transition points and recover the 9.18% onset threshold for an isolated ordinary logistic growth curve under the small-slope approximation. For a symmetric double-logistic seasonal trajectory, we derive the realized amplitude, full width at half maximum and a critical dimensionless temporal separation between growth and senescence components at which interior third-derivative extrema merge. Exact curvature-change transition points also depend on the metric assigned to the time and response axes. Local noise propagation and 4,800 nonlinear fits show how trajectory geometry affects date uncertainty: additional shape flexibility can reduce bias while increasing uncertainty in the seasonal tails. Together, these results explain how trajectory shape determines the location and existence of phenological transition points and uncertainty in their estimated dates. The framework supports phenology retrieval that preserves the underlying trajectory and interprets each metric through its mathematical definition and uncertainty.

title: Geometry-Adaptive Clustering on High-Dimensional Tori
summary: Multivariate angular data lie on a torus, but clustering methods often use the flat torus. We introduce curved-torus energy (CTE), a position-dependent dissimilarity based on restricted Riemannian path energy and minimization over winding classes. CTE has a certified finite winding reduction, an exact flat endpoint, a geodesic upper bound, and stability with respect to the geometry parameter. For label-free geometry selection, we propose CEHS-HM, a held-out criterion for selecting the warping parameter at a specified clustering resolution. We establish a finite-grid population-score regret bound and also consider joint geometry-resolution selection over finite candidate grids. Controlled experiments on $\mathbb{T}^3$ show that CTE agrees with the flat method at zero warping and becomes more useful as geometric warping increases. Additional experiments show that the CEHS-selected geometry should be viewed as a data-adaptive clustering choice rather than as an estimator of a generative deformation parameter. Under a product-von-Mises mechanism, the selector tends toward the flat endpoint when curvature is unnecessary. On ILE protein torsion data, the proposed method identifies a stable five-mode representation of joint backbone-side-chain conformation.

title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
summary: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.

title: Local quadratic convergence of iterated correlation matrices: bounds and counterexamples
summary: Kruskal's unpublished manuscript on CONCOR gives a local argument for convergence of successive correlations to a prescribed two-class sign pattern. We identify a failure in its stated one-step estimate and establish a replacement bound for correlation matrices in arbitrary dimension. A geometric estimate for sign-aligned centered rows yields an explicit sufficient neighbourhood of convergence and a quadratic error bound. We construct invariant families of correlation matrices with an exact scalar recurrence in every dimension at least three. These families yield counterexamples to the original estimate in every dimension at least four. The failure persists on relatively open sets of positive-definite correlation matrices. In dimensions divisible by four, an explicitly solvable subfamily provides counterexamples arbitrarily close to the prescribed fixed point and attains the asymptotic coefficient in the new bound. Quadratic order is attained by the constructed families in every dimension at least three. These counterexamples concern the quantitative estimate, not the convergence conclusion: all the exhibited trajectories converge to their prescribed sign patterns.

title: State Space Modeling of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process with Measurement Error: An Application to Microbiome Data
summary:
Understanding the temporal dynamics of the human microbiome is critical for deciphering host-microbe interactions and identifying responses to environmental or physiological disruptions. In this study, we develop a likelihood-based framework grounded in Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) state-space modeling to analyze longitudinal microbiome data. By applying log-ratio transformations to genus-level relative abundances, we accommodate the compositional nature of microbiome profiles and enable biologically interpretable inference.
  We estimate the mean reversion rate of the OU process using maximum likelihood estimation and construct profile likelihood confidence intervals to assess temporal stability. Biologically, higher estimated mean-reversion rates correspond to stronger regulatory feedback and thus greater temporal stability of the gut microbiome, whereas lower rates reflect weaker stabilization and slower recovery from perturbations. In the datasets analyzed here, most estimated mean reversion rates were between 0.12 and 0.36, corresponding to a half-life in the range 2-6 days for the system to return to the equilibrium level. These mean-reversion rates are substantially lower than previous estimates obtained from OU models that did not account for measurement error. To capture structural shifts in microbial dynamics, we propose a statistical testing procedure that compares a single-parameter model to a split-parameter model across disrupted time periods. We also propose an OUSSM to jointly model multiple microbes, taking into account the special measurement error covariance structure for log-ratio transformed data.

title: Kriging Beyond Gaussianity: Fixed-Domain Asymptotic Optimality
summary: Under squared-error loss, the optimal predictor of a non-Gaussian random field is its conditional mean, which may be difficult to compute. We consider a broad class of non-Gaussian random fields obtained by transforming finitely many independent Gaussian fields sharing a common correlation function, and study when kriging entails no first-order loss in mean squared prediction error (MSPE) under fixed-domain asymptotics. We compare the observed-data conditional mean, kriging with the observed covariance, kriging with the latent correlation, and a latent-information oracle. These predictors satisfy a finite-sample MSPE ordering. Under conditions linking transformation regularity to the high-frequency decay of the latent spectral density, all four MSPEs are asymptotically equivalent. For radially nonincreasing spectral densities with polynomial tails, the required regularity order is independent of both the spatial dimension and the number of latent fields. Exponential correlation also yields finite-sample bounds. Examples include Weibull, skew-Gaussian, and copula-based fields, while numerical comparisons illustrate finite-sample differences. Counterexamples show why covariance structure and first-order transformation regularity alone are insufficient. Finally, standardized prediction errors converge to a Gaussian scale mixture, which is standard normal exactly when the transformation's gradient norm is almost surely constant.

title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
summary: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
summary: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. title: Minimax Slope Estimation and Support Recovery under Weak Gaussian Selection
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. Complete proofs in Appendices A-G; numerical experiments in Appendices H-I; code, data and detailed simulation protocols in ancillary files
summary: In sample selection models, identifying a regression slope does not determine how accurately it can be estimated or distinguished from zero. title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data

title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
comment: R and Python package available at https://github.com/danilosarti/lepidoptera
summary: lepidoptera is an open-source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. Individual-level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population-level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre-fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. summary: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

title: Sample complexity of weak-signal latent-variable models
summary: We study parametric estimation in latent-variable models in the weak-signal regime, where a small signal-strength parameter $β$ controls the dependence of the observations on the unknown parameter. We also study the regime in which the target accuracy vanishes together with the signal strength, and show that global localization and local refinement may be governed by different likelihood orders, leading to distinct statistical scales. Finally, we apply our framework to broad classes of algebraically structured latent-variable models, including additive-noise channels and exponential-family models.

title: A multivariate index for estimating seasonal shifts from temperature curves
comment: 30 pages, 11 numbered figures, 1 table, and a graphical abstract. Revised manuscript under review at Earth Systems and Environment
summary: Seasonal timing is often studied using fixed calendar seasons, temperature thresholds, or a fixed smoothing parameter applied across all years. Warming is evident across time, whereas the clearest shift in seasonal timing emerges after the 2000s. By estimating both timing and temperature at each seasonal midpoint, SALLI locates where changes occur on the annual temperature curve, providing information that is more robust and data-driven than fixed thresholds, fixed calendar seasons, or a single smoothing choice.

summary: Learning topological structure from sparsely contaminated data requires robust statistical methods, as even a small fraction of atypical observations can substantially distort the inferred topology. We establish large-sample properties of the proposed functional, and show that the associated filtration induces stable and consistent persistence diagrams. We further derive a maximum bias bound for persistence diagrams in bottleneck distance, thereby providing a quantitative measure of the sparseness associated with topological inference. The practical utility of the methodology thorough testing of statistical hypothesis problem is illustrated for a seven-circle packing configuration under sparse contamination, where it recovers the underlying topological structure. Its applicability to real data is further demonstrated through an analysis of the M-ferritin protein structure, where the method identifies a persistent $H_2$ feature corresponding to the iron-storage cavity.

title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
summary: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.

title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures
summary: We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $χ^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. title: Financial Literacy and the Functional Shape of Subjective Time Deformation in Intertemporal Choice
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures (4 in main text, 7 in appendices)
summary: Intertemporal decisions are commonly summarized by a single discount parameter, although individuals with similar overall discounting intensity may value short-, medium-, and long-term delays differently. Individual discount trajectories were reconstructed and analyzed with function-on-scalar regression, allowing the association with financial literacy to vary across the temporal domain. Because the normalized subjective-time trajectory is not identifiable for flat or reconstruction-degenerate discount profiles, the primary functional analysis included 59 participants, while complementary analyses used the full analytical sample. The primary model provided no evidence of a robust linear association between financial literacy and subjective-time deformation. An exploratory categorical specification indicated heterogeneity across financial-literacy levels and departure from a linear-score representation, although individual contrasts were imprecise and sensitive to specification. summary: High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:β_m\in[-ε,ε]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.

title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
summary: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning

title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
summary: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $α<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in regressions involving general nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We demonstrate that the proposed methods---including IVX-based and related instrumental-variable procedures---facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes nearly and mildly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/α<d<2-1/α$, where $α\in(1,2]$. Our analysis is applicable to both parametric and kernel regression models. The finite-sample performance of the proposed methods is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study. Additionally, we provide an empirical application to the predictability of stock returns using long-memory heavy-tailed predictors.

summary: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.

summary: Empirical studies have identified power-law scaling and long-memory dynamics in Bitcoin prices. As a starting point, we introduce a PLT driven by a Wiener process, where the log-price follows a trend linear in log time. We explicitly derive the SDE solution, provide estimation procedures, and analyze its asymptotic properties. We extend the framework to more general driving noises. A Levy-driven PLT incorporates jump behavior, whereas fractional Brownian motion captures long-range dependence. The model is extended with a power-law volatility. We present a Monte Carlo simulation study that explores the estimator's applicability under jump-diffusion, Variance Gamma, alpha-stable, and fBm noise, and under daily, weekly, and monthly sampling. To highlight our framework's applicability, we model daily Bitcoin prices, compare the PLT model with geometric Brownian motion, and select the driving noise using out-of-sample Monte Carlo forecasting.

summary: Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. summary: Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.

title: Quantifying Uncertainty Bounds in Spectral Shallow Water Bathymetry: The Profile Likelihood Framework for Semi-Analytical Models
summary:
Accurate bathymetric mapping in shallow waters is critical for coastal monitoring, navigation safety, and environmental conservation. While semi-analytical (SA) models have proven effective for estimating water column depth (WCD) from optical remote sensing data, quantifying the associated uncertainties remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a unified framework based on profile likelihood to evaluate WCD uncertainties in Semi-Analytical (SA) models, bridging traditional variance-covariance methods with likelihood-based inference. Through controlled simulations, we systematically assess the performance of first-order statistical tests-likelihood ratio, Wald (observed and expected), and score tests-across varying environmental conditions and sensor configurations.

Our results demonstrate that the expected Fisher information Wald test, equivalent to classical variance-covariance propagation, provides reliable uncertainty bounds in hyperspectral settings with clear waters. However, its performance deteriorates in multispectral applications and complex water conditions, where likelihood ratio tests prove more robust. This divergence highlights fundamental limitations in the small-sample regime typical of per-pixel spectral bathymetry. Notably, even under idealized conditions with true parameter initialization, local optimization challenges in SA models can compromise both parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, suggesting even greater challenges in practical applications with less favorable initialization. The findings underscore the importance of robust statistical inference in improving the reliability of bathymetric products for operational applications.

summary: First-order minimaxity offers limited guidance for choosing among global-local shrinkage priors, since different local-tail distributions can yield the same leading risk. Comparisons at a common global scale may also be misleading, as the scale interacts with the shape of the local prior. We study the worst-case squared-error risks of posterior means in sparse Gaussian normal-means estimation, allowing each prior its own risk-minimizing global scale. For local-variance priors with polynomial tails and logarithmic corrections, we characterize the calibrations that retain first- and second-order minimaxity and derive the asymptotic form of the unrestricted oracle scale. Even after this optimization, differences in risk remain. The polynomial tail index, logarithmic tail exponent and a scale-invariant higher-order correction distinguish priors at successively finer orders. In particular, the horseshoe has smaller asymptotic oracle risk than the horseshoe+, despite the latter's additional logarithmic tail factor. We also establish the calibration accuracy needed to preserve these differences and sufficient conditions for their stability under high-dimensional Gaussian regression designs.

summary: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal. Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.

title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization
summary: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.

title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
summary: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

summary: Bayes factors are a widely used model comparison criterion, but are often quite challenging and computationally expensive to estimate well. We choose samples whose density in $β$ is proportional to the standard deviation of previously drawn samples. Rather than averaging many samples at each $β$, we use a very dense set of $β$ values, collecting one sample at each in order of increasing $β$ and one sample at each in order of decreasing $β$ to minimize "thermic lag". title: Weak Limits of Parameter Estimation in Strongly Identifiable Mixture Models
summary: We study the asymptotic behavior of global maximum likelihood estimation in finite mixtures with an unknown number of components bounded by \(k\). title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes

summary: This paper studies the problem of structural identifiability for graphical discrete Lyapunov models in the non-Gaussian setting from observational data. title: The Geometry of Informativeness: A Bregman-Centroid Diagnostic for Partial Pooling in Multisite Trials
summary: Two multisite trials can have the same informativeness yet differ in how reliably individual site effects can be estimated. An online credit recovery trial illustrates the diagnostics and their conditional posterior uncertainty. We recommend reporting informativeness with arithmetic mean reliability and profile dispersion. The accompanying R package poolinfo provides tools for computing the diagnostics, posterior summaries, and design calculations.

summary:

It is shown that for Dunnett's procedure AR(1), the Toeplitz band, alternating ante-dependence, and the random slope have roots below the ordinary analysis-of-variance value, while heterogeneous compound symmetry and heteroscedastic groups have roots above that value. The reduction stops for asymmetric overlap of four or more treatments, for four or more autoregressive or unstructured follow-up times, for pair-dependent variances or correlated disjoint pairs, and for a separate variance estimate in each group.

title: Correcting Bartlett factor-score error for latent covariates in partially linear double machine learning

summary: Substituting Bartlett factor scores for latent covariates leaves factor-score error that does not vanish as the sample grows and biases the adjusted structural coefficient. Residual bias after correction comes from learning the conditional means of the factor scores: signal learning error, and noise fitting, in which the learner also fits the factor-score error. Signal learning error largely cancels when the three conditional means share a common penalty, and noise fitting by a linear smoother can be computed from its weights alone, so we also subtract it (Croon-DML-R). Across 12 Monte Carlo conditions, Croon-DML reduced the absolute bias of uncorrected DML by 66-95%, and the bias of Croon-DML-R with a common penalty differed from that of an oracle estimator using the true latent variables by at most 0.004. In an illustration with public longitudinal data, the correction was 15% of the latent-covariate adjustment; its size reflected the latent-covariate coefficients rather than the residualized reliabilities.

We identify a group-wise Bernstein condition under which the same adaptive predictor attains the fast rate $1/n$ without knowing whether the condition holds, while retaining the slow rates on the groups where it fails. The condition is implied by some natural assumptions weaker than realizability. Lower bounds show that weakened versions leave every learner with slow rates. Intermediate rates under relaxed conditions and an extension to VC classes are also obtained.

title: Singularities of Multidimensional Item Response Models and the Rank of the Fisher Information Matrix
summary: Statistical models in item response theory are known to be singular. This singularity manifests itself as a loss of rank in the Fisher information matrix, and the usual theories underlying AIC and BIC, which assume regularity, cannot be applied without further justification. Chen and colleagues analyzed this degeneracy and nonregular likelihood ratio tests, but their analysis does not identify all the directions that produce degeneracy or their dimensions. In this study, we analyze the entire kernel of the Fisher information matrix as a linear space for multidimensional item response models, separating the degeneracy due to rotations from that due to an over-specified latent dimension without double counting. We determine the dimension of each component and the exact rank of the information matrix, and prove a formula for computing, from the item parameters, the dimension of the degeneracy that remains after these components are removed. These results go beyond establishing the existence of singularity to identifying its causes and extent, providing a foundation for inference and model comparison in IRT.

title: Nesting or resolution? Facility proxies for variance estimation versus confounding adjustment in claims data without facility identifiers
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material is provided as an ancillary file
summary: In claims databases, facility identifiers are often removed during de-identification, leaving only coarse attributes such as bed size. Yet facility information is needed for variance estimation, confounding adjustment and assessment of treatment availability. We examined whether accreditation-gated billing items can build strata standing for hospitals, and how to construct a facility proxy for each use. In 1,730,736 adults undergoing surgery (Medical Data Vision database, Japan, 2019-2023), we built marker-pattern strata from 66 accreditation-gated receipt codes (markers) and evaluated each grouping against a true facility identifier in an insurer-based database (DeSC Healthcare) and in simulation. The variance explained by the marker-pattern strata decreased with the extent to which a variable was patient- rather than hospital-determined ($R^2$ 0.921 for an accreditation item, 0.036 for sex). For variance estimation, the supplied-attribute cells, which can merge but never split hospitals, kept the type I error rate at 4.8% with a wild cluster bootstrap, against 5.4% for the true identifier and 39% when clustering was ignored; every finer marker-based grouping did worse. For adjustment, evaluated with real facility-level confounders and simulated null exposures, the marker pattern removed 51% of the confounding related to accreditation-linked facility characteristics, against 8% for the cells. The proportion of patients in groups mixing hospitals with and without the relevant accreditation was 49% for the marker pattern against 98% for the cells. No single facility proxy serves every purpose: nesting governs variance estimation, and resolution governs adjustment and treatment availability. Without a facility identifier, the supplied-attribute cells can carry the standard errors, and marker-pattern strata are worth considering for the other two uses.

summary: The LR1 distribution links an exponential lifetime and a four-stage gamma lifetime through a single positive parameter $λ$. title: Selecting the Best Few with Human Evaluators: Adaptively Combining Ratings and Pairwise Comparisons
summary: This paper considers a decision-maker tasked with identifying the $k$ best items from a large pool of candidates, such as job applicants, LLMs, award nominees, or new product ideas. The decision-maker learns about the items' quality by soliciting human evaluations. Each evaluation can be costly, so the decision-maker aims to use the limited evaluation budget efficiently by allocating evaluations adaptively. A key consideration is the form of evaluation to solicit, which should be something evaluators are comfortable providing. Two popular forms are ratings and pairwise comparisons, and we allow for both, as they may be especially useful in combination given the limited budget. Ratings can be used early on to get a coarse picture of which items are good and which are not. As that picture forms, comparisons can refine the ordering of the good items, narrowing in on the ultimate top-$k$ selection. To solve the allocation problem, we develop an adaptive algorithm built from two allocation policies. The first, our primary contribution, is based on a surrogate objective that is naturally forward-looking, valuing evaluations that help inform what to evaluate in future rounds, not just those that directly improve the selection decision. The decision rule is interpretable, and we prove that it is asymptotically consistent. Late in the evaluation process, when being forward-looking is less productive, we construct a myopic policy and a criterion for switching to it. In simulation, the method gives insight into how to combine these two types of evaluations, and beats the (limited) existing benchmarks.

title: Inconsistency between Frequentist and Bayesian inference, approximation of improper priors and permissible priors
summary:

Through continuous and discrete examples, we show that EKL convergence can depend on the sequence of compact sets used for approximation. In particular, convergence along one compact exhaustion need not extend to others.

Consequently, KL-permissible and TV permissible priors cannot be strongly inconsistent. We also introduce weak inconsistency and show that it may persist despite EKL convergence. Finally, a unified discrete framework covering the Flatland and Fraser-Monette-Ng paradoxes illustrates the distinction between these notions. In particular, ETV convergence need not imply EKL convergence, while the absence of weak inconsistency does not guarantee an EKL convergent compact approximation.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
comment: 50 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Extended version of a paper accepted at ICAIF 2026 Workshop on AI-Driven Market Microstructure. MSc dissertation, London School of Economics and Political Science (2026)
summary: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences
summary: We extend anytime-valid inference for linear models from independent scalar outcomes to units that contribute a vector of dependent outcomes. title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes
summary: Joint-life insurance often involves several lifetimes subject to censoring at known dates. We construct prediction regions by reducing the lifetime vector to a suitable scalar outcome. title: Teacher Supervision, Fixed Representations and Calibration: Exact Risk Calculations for Candidate-Scoring Decision Models
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code in ancillary files
summary: Candidate-scoring decision models return a probability distribution over a presented set of answers. summary: We propose the Vector Copula-based Markov Model (VCBMM) for describing multivariate time series with nonlinear dependence. The performance of the proposed model is illustrated through simulation studies. In real data analysis, we apply the model to bivariate daily stock returns from the 2008 global financial crisis (2008 GFC) and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic (2020 COVID-19).

title: Dimension-free comparison inequalities between $f$-divergences for Gaussian location mixtures
summary: We establish dimension-free comparison inequalities between the Kullback-Leibler (KL) and $χ^2$-divergences and the squared Hellinger distance for Gaussian location mixtures with compactly supported mixing distributions. We show that both divergences are bounded by the squared Hellinger distance up to constants depending only on the radius of the support, independently of the ambient dimension and the number of mixture components. These results resolve an open question raised by \cite{jia2023entropic} and strengthen existing comparison inequalities. Our proof relies on a Gaussian interpolation argument that relates the derivatives of these divergences to differences between posterior means.

title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
summary: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
summary: Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.

summary: We study mediation and moderation in the distance-based regression model for triangular fuzzy responses, in which the center and transformed spreads of the response are linear in the components of fuzzy and crisp covariates. Moderation is modeled through triangular interaction regressors and tested with a Freedman--Lane permutation test. In simulations calibrated on real data, percentile bootstrap intervals for the indirect effects had coverage between 0.905 and 0.975, the empirical size of the indirect-effect tests did not exceed 0.085, and ignoring the paths through the mediator spreads biased the indirect effect on the center by 16 to 20\% at every sample size. summary: In randomized trials, outcome assessment times often vary across participants and may depend on the underlying outcome process, so outcomes observed near a target time need not represent the target population. Whether assessment is informative cannot be determined from the observed data alone. We extend the sensitivity analysis framework of Smith et al.\ (2024), which is anchored in an explainable assessment assumption and was restricted to continuous outcomes through an identity-link marginal mean model, to a broader class of link functions that accommodates binary and count outcomes. Within this framework, we develop an influence function-based augmented inverse intensity-weighted estimator that is root-$n$ consistent under standard regularity conditions. We also propose a data-driven procedure for selecting the range of the sensitivity parameter from plausible bounds on the target mean outcome and for constructing a confidence set for this range, which accounts for uncertainty in sensitivity parameter selection. We illustrate the method with data from the ARC study and evaluate its finite-sample performance in simulation studies.

Under an additional orthogonality condition, we identify the causal prediction function as the unique risk minimiser subject to this invariance restriction. We establish consistency and an explicit rate, derive a goodness-of-fit test for the invariance restriction, and characterise the population target under misspecification. The finite-sample behavior of the proposed methodology is investigated through simulation experiments under Gaussian, contaminated, and heavy-tailed settings. An application to daily returns of three major cryptocurrencies illustrates its practical utility on financial data.

With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.

summary: Expected shortfall is defined as the truncated mean of a random variable that falls below a specified quantile level and is widely recognized as an important risk measure. Our empirical results on stock market data indicate that the proposed models effectively capture the clustering patterns and leverage effects on the conditional expected shortfall.

summary: Organ transplantation evaluation is a multi-stage process in which only patients who complete one stage remain eligible for the next, leading to patient attrition and reducing later-stage sample sizes. title: Where to weight? Estimating population causal effects with weighted double score matching in complex surveys

summary: Double score matching is an emerging method for causal inference that combines propensity and prognostic scores to achieve dimension reduction and model robustness. Applications to early marijuana use and mental health in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health and to sleep duration and glycemic control in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey illustrate the practical value of WDSM for population-level inference. We conclude with a discussion of our findings and provide practical guidance on incorporating survey weights into matching-based analyses of observational data.

Numerical results on an educational survey quantify the impact of budget and quality constraints on estimation precision and demonstrate how the trade-off information guides iterative refinement of preference weightings.

title: Covariate-adaptive randomization using historical data and bootstrap-based inference
comment: Theoretical results to be added soon
summary: Covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR) can improve the efficiency of average treatment effect (ATE) estimation by reducing chance imbalances in prognostic baseline covariates. A recently proposed CAR method that balances multiple covariates, including continuous ones, can achieve optimal precision when the conditional mean of the outcome can be expressed as a linear combination of the covariate features used for the CAR procedure. However, this condition may be difficult to satisfy when the relationship between covariates and the outcome is nonlinear. Furthermore, directly balancing multiple covariates may reduce estimation precision in finite samples. We propose three CAR methods that incorporate a prognostic score learned from individual-level historical data into their imbalance measures. The prognostic score reduces multiple covariates to one dimension while giving larger weights to covariates that are more strongly associated with the outcome. Another challenge with CAR is difficulty in inference due to dependence between subjects induced by the CAR procedure. Existing bootstrap-based inference methods emulate the CAR design by reassigning treatment within each bootstrap sample, which causes difficulty in interval estimation under CAR with continuous covariates. We propose a bootstrap method with unequal probability resampling corresponding to the CAR design, avoiding reassignment within each bootstrap sample. In simulations, the proposed CAR methods reduced prognostic imbalance, thereby improving estimation precision compared to existing assignment designs, and the proposed bootstrap method accurately assessed estimation uncertainty under our proposed CAR. An application to Clazosentan trials demonstrated that the proposed CAR methods similarly improved prognostic balance, and the proposed bootstrap method closely reproduced the distribution induced by the proposed CAR.

summary: Disentangling therapist from intervention effects has long been considered a challenge in randomised trials of therapist delivered interventions. In practice, these are strong assumptions that may lead to delayed or suspended randomisation and increased trial costs. We propose three novel randomisation strategies that explicitly account for therapist capacity, availability, and turnover while maintaining desirable statistical properties. In a simulation study, we compared the proposed and existing randomisation strategies across trial scenarios and design parameters, assessing trade offs between operational efficiency and statistical performance. The results provide practical guidance for trialists designing trials of therapist delivered interventions under real world constraints.
