Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.

title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
summary: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

title: Computational Taxonomy for visualizing and exploring systems with functional response dynamics: soybean's O2-respiration example
summary: A collective of 1684 O2-respiration curves of 183 dimensions are collected along soybeans' germinating process with 72 covariate feature-measurements. We develop a computational thematic platform for first discovering and exposing heterogeneous typical-shapes and then extracting readable, visible and explainable pattern information with biological implications when comparing between them. Via existing knowledge on seeds of much smaller sizes, such collective of O2-respiration curves are expected to generally embrace the two-stage or sigmoidal patterns. However, due to Soybean's relatively large surface area with harder to control and retain experimental conditions, much diverse and heterogeneous shapes are highly expected. Shannon entropy is applied to capture potential categorical nature across the 183 time-points, while scaled mutual information is used to evaluate pattern-consistency. Three motifs are determined to partition the temporal time-points into three regions: W1 on [1, 20], W2 on [21, 60] and W3 on [61, 183]. Each curve is partitioned into three segments accordingly. Hierarchical cluster algorithm is applied onto these motif-region-specific curve-segments, respectively. Five clusters of shapes on W1 are selected, four on W2 and four on W3. We computationally build a tree-geometry-based Taxonomic Hierarchy to organize these 80 curve-shapes into 15 typical shapes. Then we compare among these typical shapes to extract and display their differences through block-sustained heatmaps. Each focal block is expressed va a network of covariate features to reveal dominant interacting effects of various orders. Scientific explanations and understanding are to be rested on the collected heatmaps and coupled networks collectively.

title: Local Manifold Attention for Recovery and Generation of Rare 3D Human Poses
summary: A rare 3D human pose in a motion sequence may reflect either a genuine movement or an estimation error, making correction difficult when reference databases contain few comparable examples. We investigate whether local geometric structure can support the recovery and generation of rare configura- tions, using motion-capture sequences from AMASS, which unifies datasets through a common parametric human-body model, together with video-based pose estimates. We develop the cylindrical manifold attention transformer (CMAT), which extends local manifold fitting through geometry- and task- dependent neighborhood weights. For motion correction, Self-Action CMAT draws on comparable windows within a sequence, adjusts their contributions for neighborhood imbalance and temporal dependence, and integrates local geometry with robust temporal regularization. Experiments on perturbed and estimated motions show reductions in position and acceleration errors, with component analyses examining how weighting and temporal processing con- tribute to recovery. The controlled correction comparisons are exploratory and conditional on the selected motion-amplitude bound. For generation, Rarity-preserving CMAT explores locally supported configurations subject to independently calibrated rarity and separation from stored observations. Under common screening criteria, it achieves a higher yield of eligible rare poses than the evaluated generation baselines.

title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
summary: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
summary: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

title: Efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence
summary: Measures of functional dependence that characterize both independence and perfect dependence have attracted growing interest. Despite their appealing theoretical properties, existing rank- and graph-based estimators can suffer from substantial bias under general dependence, limiting their usefulness for statistical inference. Moreover, a systematic and practically accessible framework for mitigating such bias while achieving semiparametric efficiency remains largely unavailable. In this paper, we develop a general framework for efficient estimation of measures of functional dependence through sample-splitting and cross-fitting. Our approach enables systematic bias reduction and semiparametrically efficient inference, and thus offers a flexible and theoretically grounded alternative to existing rank- and graph-based methods.

title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Efficiency Characterization
summary: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach uses an $F$-weighted portfolio with a predefined prior $F$. For suitable priors, this approach has recently been shown to achieve the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, the prior $F$ changes how the portfolio test behaves near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and introduce an efficiency measure that allows the error probability and alternative to vary jointly. Under mild assumptions, we prove that efficiency equals a logarithmic decay index of the prior near zero. This gives a necessary and sufficient condition for optimality: Beta priors have infinite efficiency, whereas suitable Robbins-type priors attain efficiency 1. As an application, we consider testing a specified mean of a bounded random variable and describe an implementation of the portfolio algorithm with almost-linear computational complexity.

title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
summary: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

title: R2-GP: Variance-Calibrated Priors for Additive Gaussian Processes
summary: We develop R2-GP, an R2D2-type prior for Gaussian process (GP) generalised additive models (GAMs) that calibrates explained variance ($R^2$) for Matérn covariance kernels. The function variance for standard Matérn kernels depends jointly on the effect magnitude and length-scale. As such, smooth and rough components with identical amplitudes contribute very different amounts of variation. With independent priors on component amplitudes, this variation results in variance overestimation, especially in higher dimensions. We overcome this by taking direct control over each component's expected contribution to prior explained variance. We do this by rescaling each component based on its length scale and observed inputs, and modelling each rescaled variance as a share of the function variance induced by a global $R^2$ prior. This allows R2-GP to scale well to many components. To also scale to large sample sizes, we extend R2-GP to Hilbert space approximation methods, a framework for kernels exploiting their spectral decompositions for fast and efficient inference. Our simulations and real-world case studies demonstrate superior generalisation and parameter recovery over independent variance priors.
